"""
# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.
"""

# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.
"""

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.

# Source comparison: report 1

Draft: scratch/write-k3zkeg/draft.md
Source (brief and material): work/source.md
Language: draft sv, source sv. The one quotation is quoted in the original language and is not translated.

## Claim accounting

Each item gives the draft passage (D), the source passage it rests on (S), what differs, and the result.

### Title
D: "Tallmora Energi inviger solpark på gamla grustäkten vid Kvarnbacken"
S: "Tallmora Energi AB inviger solparken vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora den 3 juni 2027. Parken ligger på den mark där kommunens grustäkt låg fram till 2019." / "Grustäkten vid Kvarnbacken avvecklades 2019."
Differences: The draft drops "AB", which names the same company. "gamla grustäkten" (the former gravel pit) comes from "låg fram till 2019" and "avvecklades 2019". Ekholm uses the same wording herself: "en gammal grustäkt". The present-tense "inviger" for a future event matches the brief's own wording ("inviger ... den 3 juni 2027"), and the body gives the date. I found no case where one statement holds and the other fails. Supported.

### Lead paragraph
1. D: "Den 3 juni 2027 invigs Tallmora Energi AB:s solpark vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora."
   S: "Tallmora Energi AB inviger solparken vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora den 3 juni 2027."
   Differences: The draft uses the passive without an agent, so it does not say who performs the inauguration. That is weaker than the source, not different from it, and the title names Tallmora Energi as the one inaugurating. The draft makes ownership explicit with the genitive "AB:s". This rests on the brief's "Tallmora Energi AB inviger solparken" and "fick tillstånd att bygga solparken". Supported.
2. D: "Parken ligger där kommunens grustäkt låg fram till 2019"
   S: "Parken ligger på den mark där kommunens grustäkt låg fram till 2019."
   Differences: "där" versus "på den mark där" gives the same location. Supported.
3. D: "har 12 000 solpaneler på 18 hektar och har kostat 64 miljoner kronor att bygga."
   S: "Den har 12 000 solpaneler på 18 hektar och har kostat 64 miljoner kronor att bygga."
   Differences: none. Supported.
4. D: "Bolaget beräknar att den ger 7,5 gigawattimmar el om året."
   S: "Bolaget beräknar att parken ger 7,5 gigawattimmar el om året"
   Differences: The draft keeps "beräknar" (estimates), so the company is the one asserting the figure and it stays an estimate. The explicit qualification "Siffran är en uppskattning ..." comes two paragraphs later (see item 7). Because "beräknar" is kept, the lead does not state the figure as fact. Pronoun "den": its referent is "parken", third person singular. It has grammatical common (utrum) gender only and makes no natural-gender assertion. The source uses the same pronoun for the same referent ("Den har ..."). Supported.

### Quotation
5. D: "– Solparken visar att en gammal grustäkt kan göra nytta igen, och vi vill att elen som används i Tallmora också ska produceras här, säger Maria Ekholm, vd för Tallmora Energi."
   S: "Vd Maria Ekholm säger: ”Solparken visar att en gammal grustäkt kan göra nytta igen, och vi vill att elen som används i Tallmora också ska produceras här.”"
   Differences: The quoted words match the source word for word. There is no repair, no translation, and no change to hedge, stance or wording. "vi" is first person plural and is the speaker's own word, unchanged. The draft adds that she is "vd för Tallmora Energi". The brief says only "Vd" but gives it inside Tallmora Energi AB's own press-release brief, and her "vi" refers to the operator of the park. The supplied context settles her company, and I could name no case compatible with the material in which she is vd of a different organisation. The draft uses no personal pronoun for Ekholm and asserts no natural gender. Supported. Quotation approval is outside this check.

### Household equivalence and uncertainty
6. D: "Enligt bolagets egen beräkning motsvarar 7,5 gigawattimmar hushållselen i omkring 1 500 villor."
   S: "... 7,5 gigawattimmar el om året, vilket enligt bolagets egen beräkning motsvarar hushållselen i omkring 1 500 villor."
   Differences: The draft keeps the attribution ("enligt bolagets egen beräkning") and the approximation ("omkring"). This sentence does not repeat "om året", but it follows directly from the lead's "7,5 gigawattimmar el om året", so an ordinary reader takes the same annual quantity. The scope is unchanged. Supported.
7. D: "Siffran är en uppskattning, och den verkliga produktionen beror på hur soligt året blir."
   S: "Siffran är en uppskattning; den verkliga produktionen beror på hur soligt året blir."
   Differences: A semicolon becomes a comma plus "och". In both texts "Siffran" follows a sentence that contains both 7.5 GWh and 1 500 villas, so its referent is exactly as open as in the source. Supported.

### Delivery and access
8. D: "Elen levereras till elnätet, och parken säljer ingen el direkt till hushållen i närheten."
   S: "Elen levereras till elnätet. Parken säljer ingen el direkt till hushållen i närheten."
   Differences: none. Supported.
9. D: "Området är inhägnat och inte öppet för allmänheten, utom vid invigningen den 3 juni klockan 14.00–16.00, då bolaget visar parken för besökare."
   S: identical wording.
   Differences: none. Supported.

### Background
10. D: "Grustäkten vid Kvarnbacken avvecklades 2019."
    S: identical. Supported.
11. D: "Tallmora Energi fick tillstånd att bygga solparken 2025, och bygget började i augusti 2026."
    S: identical. Supported.
12. D: "Parken har 40 växelriktare och panelerna står i rader i öst–västlig riktning."
    S: "Parken har 40 växelriktare, panelerna står i rader i öst–västlig riktning"
    Differences: none of substance. Supported.
13. D: "Marken mellan raderna betas av får från en gård i närheten."
    S: "markytan mellan raderna betas av får från en gård i närheten."
    Differences: "Marken" versus "markytan" names the same ground between the rows. Supported.

### Pictures, contact and about the company
14. D: "Bilder från solparken: https://example.se/press/kvarnbacken-bilder"
    S: "Bilder från solparken finns på https://example.se/press/kvarnbacken-bilder." Same URL. Supported.
15. D: "Presskontakt: Lina Sjögren, kommunikationschef, Tallmora Energi, telefon 070-000 00 00"
    S: "Kontakt för redaktioner: Lina Sjögren, kommunikationschef, Tallmora Energi, telefon 070-000 00 00."
    Differences: "Presskontakt" versus "Kontakt för redaktioner". Given the brief's stated audience (local and regional newsrooms), I found no concrete case in which she is one and not the other. Name, title and number are identical. Supported.
16. D: "Tallmora Energi AB ägs av Tallmora kommun och levererar el och fjärrvärme till omkring 14 000 kunder i kommunen."
    S: identical ("Om bolaget: ..."). Supported.

## Pronoun accounting
- "den" (lead): refers to "parken"; third person singular; grammatical common gender only; no natural-gender claim. The source uses the same.
- "vi" (quotation): the speaker's own first person plural, unchanged from the source.
- Maria Ekholm and Lina Sjögren have no personal pronouns anywhere in the draft, so the draft makes no natural-gender assertion about either person.

## Findings

Source-support findings: none.
Translation findings: none. The quotation is not translated and matches the source word for word.

## Completion status
Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the draft, including the title, has a matching source passage with no change in subject, scope, time, modality, certainty or attribution. No findings are unresolved.
